chapter: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
title: Claim that Black bands heard the Dixieland records and copied them
summary: He argues the banjo and rhythm on the Oliver record were taken from the Dixieland recordings and makes demeaning remarks about Black musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You heard it. Now, had these Negroes or Eagles came to New York, before they heard the Dixieland band record, they would have been thrown on the ears, not shoved out the door, but thrown out bodily. Now, I'm going to go to this spot where he makes his clarinet solo. You'll notice that the banjo simulates a saxophone slap-tonment. They must have heard this St. Louis blues record, because it's almost identically like it. You hear the banjo simulates a slap-ton on a saxophone. Now, that rhythm they play is Dixieland's stop. The last ending of the Dixieland recorders. Well, let's get to the clarinet part. Let me see if I can find it now. I'll have to pick up this foolish thing in there. This is the St. Louis blues, man. And your head of the Negro plays is in this record. There's a slap-tonment. These records were made six years before the Negroes recorded this.

Every Negro banded everyone out, but Louis Armstrong and all of them, they held higher, higher, higher. They got it out the Dixieland record. Now, you don't mean to tell me we just come from a London area, and we could have heard the Negroes playing in New Orleans. That's impossible. They heard this record.

That's the rhythm they use. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da. You leave out the last note. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. That's how ignorant the Negroes walk. And you have many white crowns. That's how ignorant too.
I'm trying to get excited now.
